title: Map-tile mipmaps: multi-resolution embeddings split across DRAM and flash
idea: Like web maps loading coarse tiles before fine ones, store a 4-bit coarse version of each embedding or retrieval vector in DRAM and its residual refinement levels on flash; the model uses the coarse level by default and fetches residuals only when a confidence check fails.
why: Most lookups are satisfied at the coarse level; ~4x less DRAM for large embedding and retrieval indexes with flash serving <10% of reads.

title: Bell Labs 1952 ferroelectric matrix read by small-signal capacitance
idea: Revive Anderson's transistor-less ferroelectric crossbar in sputtered HZO or sol-gel PZT, but read it without switching: a small AC probe senses the polarization-dependent capacitance (the C-V butterfly asymmetry, enhanced by an imprint layer), so reads are non-destructive and fatigue-free, and V/3 biasing limits half-select disturb on rare writes.
why: A transistor-free 4F^2 stackable crossbar with unlimited reads and no restore holds read-mostly AI data outside DRAM, built with ALD/sputter and two metal layers.

title: Molybdenite exfoliation: peel only the bit-planes a token needs
idea: MoS2 peels into single layers; weights are stored bit-plane-major in row-aligned tiles (all MSBs of a tile together, then the next bit), and a per-token difficulty predictor fetches 2, 3, 4 or 8 planes, so easy tokens run a lower-precision model from the same single copy without overfetching unused planes.
why: Fetching 2-3 planes for most decode steps instead of 16-bit weights cuts weight bits moved ~6-8x on average and >10x on easy tokens, and LSB planes of cold layers can be evicted to flash (energy, density).

title: Swap SSD DRAM mapping tables for learned piecewise-linear FTL in SRAM
idea: Substitute the SSD's DRAM logical-to-physical map (~1 GB per TB) with a learned index of piecewise-linear segments held in controller SRAM. The FTL lays out writes in a log-structured way to keep segments long, and a small exact table catches outliers.
why: Enterprise SSDs use a noticeable share of DRAM bit shipments (exabytes of flash at 1 GB/TB). A 50-200x smaller map removes nearly all SSD DRAM and returns that supply to servers.

title: Swap 64-bit pointers for region-relative 32-bit pointer instructions
idea: Substitute absolute 64-bit pointers with hardware base-plus-offset addressing. New load and store instructions take a 32-bit offset from a per-region base register with a hardware bounds check, so C/C++ compilers can emit 32-bit pointers in heaps above 4 GB without software decode overhead.
why: Pointer-dense heaps (graphs, trees, object stores, databases) shrink 25-40%. Compressed oops already proves this in software, and the hardware path brings it to native code.

title: Segment-base hardware makes 32-bit compressed pointers universal
idea: Combine x86-style segment base registers with pointer compression: the load/store unit adds a per-region base plus a 3-bit shift to 32-bit references in a single cycle, so C/C++/Rust allocators and runtimes can use compressed pointers in any heap, not only JVM/V8-style ones.
why: Pointer-heavy structures (graphs, trees, ASTs, indexes) shrink 30-40%.

title: Segment:offset 32-bit relative pointers for in-memory data structures
idea: TRIZ #35 Parameter change: like 8086 segment:offset addressing, data structures store 32-bit (or 16-bit) offsets relative to a segment base held in FS/GS or a register, inside 4 GB arenas, halving pointer width; compilers emit base-plus-offset loads at ~1 cycle of cost.
why: Pointers are 30-50% of graph, tree and object heaps; 15-30% total heap reduction on existing CPUs.

title: Experts stored as shared base plus low-rank deltas
idea: MoE experts and per-tenant fine-tunes are highly correlated, so their joint information is far less than N full matrices. Factor each expert as W_base + A_i B_i (rank 32-128) and compute x.W_base + (x.A_i).B_i on the fly, so memory holds one base and N small deltas.
why: 5-10x smaller expert and multi-tenant fine-tune memory, for a few percent extra FLOPs.

title: Near-duplicate KV blocks share a base plus 4-bit residual
idea: Box: approximate dedup × GPU KV pool × 16-token block × LSH on key vectors × shared base + sparse quantized residual. Blocks from different requests (edited system prompts, popular RAG documents, boilerplate code) whose keys fall within a tolerance are stored once with tiny per-request residuals.
why: Exact prefix sharing misses near-duplicates; merging them adds 1.5–3× effective KV capacity in RAG and agent serving.

title: Charge sharing rebuilds rows from a base row plus deltas
idea: Store groups of similar rows (neighboring embedding vectors, image tiles) as one full-precision base row plus low-bit delta rows. On read, the subarray opens the base and delta rows together onto shared bitlines with binary-weighted capacitive coupling, so charge redistribution adds them in analog before sensing. Decompression happens inside the mat with no logic.
why: Gives 1.5-3x effective capacity for redundant data at zero periphery cost (facts 7, 8).

title: Hydrogen isotopes: near-duplicate pages stored as base plus neutron delta
idea: Like protium vs deuterium (same element, one extra neutron), the memory controller finds pages that differ from an existing base page in only a few bytes (forked VMs, container images, agent sandboxes, model replicas with patched metadata) using 64-bit similarity sketches, and stores them as a base pointer plus a <=256 B XOR delta. Reads rebuild lines in a delta-apply unit; writes that grow the delta past a threshold trigger a copy-on-write split.
why: Exact dedup (KSM) only catches identical pages (~5-15% in clouds); near-duplicate capture adds ~15-30% more effective capacity on VM/container/agent fleets, about 1.3-1.6x less DRAM per host (cost/bit).

title: Buckled AlN micro-beams store compression codebooks with zero leakage
idea: Weight-clustering codebooks and LZ dictionaries (a few hundred KB, rarely updated) are stored as up/down buckled states of AlN-actuated micro-beams next to the decompression engine. A piezo pulse snaps a beam and capacitive sensing reads it. With no charge to leak, 125 C for 10 years is a non-issue, whereas SRAM leaks heavily at that temperature and loses its contents at power-off.
why: The whole model can stay 4-8x compressed in memory with its codebook always on-die, cutting DRAM capacity 3-6x in hot ECUs.

title: Retrain tokenizers for fewer tokens per document, shrinking KV
idea: Box: fewer tokens × tokenizer × token × next model refresh × larger multilingual/code-aware vocabulary with frequent multi-word merges. New model generations adopt tokenizers that encode the same text in 20–30% fewer tokens, and KV size scales with token count.
why: 20–30% less KV per context at long context, outweighing the larger embedding table; software only, no fluorinated chemistry.

title: IBM expanded storage, fixed: synchronous page-move to a cheap tier
idea: IBM mainframe Expanded Storage (1985-2000s) was a cheaper DRAM tier reached by a synchronous page-move instruction, retired when 64-bit addressing made it look unnecessary. Revive it as an ISA/CXL instruction that moves a 4 KB page between near DRAM and a compressed or LPDDR far tier in ~1 us with no page fault or I/O stack.
why: Swap-in at ~1 us instead of 10-100 us lets OSes run with 30-50% smaller near DRAM and negligible stalls.

title: Electrochromic WO3 shutters hold model weights inside the photonic multiplier
idea: Each weight is a Li-intercalated WO3 attenuator on a silicon-nitride waveguide mesh. An ion-injection pulse sets its optical transmission once, and it holds without power. Activations ride on light and are multiplied as they pass through the colored film, so the weights live in the compute fabric and DRAM holds only activations and KV.
why: Weight-stationary optics takes both weight capacity and weight traffic out of DRAM (fact 5). That means 50-90% less DRAM for inference appliances whose models rarely change.

title: Interlibrary loan: one shared weight copy serving sixteen hosts
idea: Like libraries lending one rare book, place a single read-only copy of popular model weights behind a CXL 3 switch, mapped read-only into 8-16 inference hosts that each keep only a hot-layer cache; an epoch counter replaces coherence traffic because the data is immutable.
why: Inference farms replicate the same 100-800 GB of weights per host; sharing cuts weight DRAM 8-16x per pod at +100-200 ns access hidden by layer prefetch.

title: Swap greedy tensor allocators for ILP-planned rematerialization and packing
idea: Substitute runtime greedy allocation with a solved plan. One integer program over the training graph decides jointly which activations to keep, recompute or offload and their exact arena offsets, removing fragmentation and peak-coincident lifetimes before the run.
why: Training peak memory falls 2-4x versus caching allocators with heuristic checkpointing, for ~10-20% extra compute, on unchanged HBM.

title: Quench-and-temper training: harden models against the exact flip channel
idea: Steel is hardened by quenching, then tempered to remove brittleness. Models are fine-tuned with 1% bit flips injected into the exact stored bit format (the quantized codes, not the protected scales) using straight-through estimators, then 'tempered' with a short pass on clean data. The hardened model is deployed at 3 bits per weight on 1%-BER memory.
why: Fault-aware training is reported to recover much of the accuracy lost to flips, enabling about 5x weight compression on cheap unrefreshed cells and less premium HBM per inference server.

title: Vinyl-record pressing: via-programmed mask ROM for frozen model weights
idea: Borrowed from record pressing, where one stamper makes millions of discs: frozen model weights are pressed into 1-transistor mask ROM by a single cheap via/metal mask on a commodity logic wafer (no EUV, no capacitor) stacked under the accelerator, so weights need zero DRAM and zero refresh; a new model version is a new via mask.
why: Removes the weight footprint from DRAM; mask ROM is dense, has zero standby and refresh power, uses mature U.S.-available nodes and needs no capacitor or EUV.

title: Idle GPU video encoders compress the LLM KV cache
idea: Combine the motion-compensated inter-frame prediction of on-die AV1/HEVC encoders with attention KV tensors: treat each head's K/V across successive token blocks as video frames, encode residuals in the otherwise idle media engine, and decode blocks back into HBM just before attention reads them.
why: KV cache dominates inference memory; temporal and cross-head redundancy could yield 4-8x KV compression using silicon that already sits unused on datacenter GPUs (facts 5, 6).

title: Motion-compensated memory pages: shifted reference plus residual
idea: Borrowing H.264 P-frame motion compensation: a CXL memory controller finds, for each cold 4 KB page, a reference page and a byte-offset 'motion vector' (pages that match after a shift, e.g. realigned structs or shifted buffers) and stores only the vector plus an entropy-coded residual; reads reconstruct in a short pipeline from a hot reference-page cache.
why: Catches near-duplicates that exact dedup and per-line compression miss (VM images, JVM heaps, checkpoint shards); claims 1.5-3x extra capacity on cold tiers, lowering cost per usable bit.

title: Passive optical splitters copy one weight stream to many accelerators
idea: Copying a bit electrically costs CV^2 at every receiver; an optical 1:N splitter copies light passively, down to a shot-noise floor of ~100 photons per bit per receiver. Serve weights from a single pooled memory through polymer waveguides laminated into the organic board with 1:16 splitters, and synchronize the replicas so all of them read the same layer at the same moment.
why: Data-parallel replicas stop holding private weight copies, so weight memory per replica falls up to 16x; each extra receiver costs ~0.1 pJ/bit vs ~1-3 pJ/bit electrically.

title: Single MIM-capacitor mask giving SoCs a compression-metadata eDRAM
idea: One BEOL MIM-capacitor mask added to the CPU/GPU logic process yields dense 1T1C eDRAM at about 3x SRAM density. It is used only for compressed-memory metadata and translation (sector sizes, line pointers) for all of main memory. Metadata misses, the main reason compressed DRAM is slow, disappear, so 32-64 MB of on-die storage governs a TB-scale tier.
why: It makes 2-3x main-memory compression latency-neutral, so servers can install proportionally less DRAM.

title: Lisp-machine CDR-coding deletes adjacent pointers from managed heaps
idea: Generalize MIT/Symbolics Lisp-machine cdr-coding: the garbage collector lays objects out in traversal order and a 2-bit tag per word says 'next reference is the adjacent object', so the load unit synthesizes that address and the 8-byte pointer is never stored. Applies to Java/Go/Python heaps, graph databases and B-trees.
why: Pointers are 30-50% of bytes in managed heaps and graph stores, a large share of datacenter DRAM; eliding adjacent-object pointers recovers 15-30% of that capacity at near-zero CPU cost.

title: Value-range narrowing: JIT shrinks fields to the bits actually used
idea: Inverts 'a field's width is fixed by its declared type': a profiling JIT sees that int64/double fields hold small ranges (counters, enums, timestamps near now) and re-lays objects into bit-packed struct-of-arrays, with guard deoptimization if a value ever overflows.
why: Java, JS and Python heaps carry 40-70% unused high-order and padding bits; heaps shrink 1.5-2.5x with no programmer change.

title: Platinum catalyst banks: analytics filters run at the bank surface
idea: Like a catalytic converter reacting gas on the platinum surface without moving it elsewhere, each DRAM bank group gets a small predicate unit beside its sense amplifiers that decodes dictionary-compressed columns and evaluates WHERE clauses and aggregates in place; only matching row IDs or partial sums cross the I/O.
why: Off-chip I/O dominates the 10-20 pJ/bit DDR cost; scans at 1-5% selectivity move 20-100x fewer bits (>10x lower energy per useful access), and columns can stay 3-5x compressed in DRAM because decoding happens at the bank (energy, density).

title: Swap replicated cluster datasets for threads that migrate to data
idea: Substitute moving data with moving computation. On a remote access, a thread's ~200-byte context hops to the node that owns the data instead of the data being fetched or cached locally, so graph and sparse datasets are stored exactly once across the cluster.
why: Distributed graph analytics keeps 2-5x ghost and replica copies. Single-copy storage cuts cluster DRAM 2-3x for those workloads.

title: In/Ga-free zinc-silicon-oxide gain cells stacked over accelerator logic
idea: IFR: the KV cache lives on the compute die for free. The constraint bans IGZO, so use amorphous Zn-Si-O channels: 2T0C gain cells deposited below 400 C in the BEOL above the attention units, with TiN electrodes and Al2O3 gate dielectric, holding transient KV and activations for milliseconds with occasional refresh.
why: Moves the hot KV set off external HBM; if ZSO leakage approaches IGZO's, refresh becomes negligible and several GB sit on-die.

title: Alien with no CPU/memory split: attention computed in HBM logic die
idea: An alien that never separated thinking from remembering would score attention and accumulate values in the HBM base die. KV is stored in a 2-bit grouped format that only the in-stack PIM reads: dequantization and softmax happen beside the banks, and only the attended output vector leaves the stack.
why: KV capacity per stack rises 4-8x and KV traffic leaves the interposer, attacking both data-movement energy (3-4 pJ/bit) and capacity.

title: Eliminate background app residency with compressed heap hibernation on clients
idea: A desktop OS service serializes the JS/V8 heaps of background browser tabs and Electron apps into zstd blobs on SSD and restores them lazily on focus, with sub-second resume.
why: Electron apps and tabs consume 300 MB-1 GB each; laptops could ship 8 GB instead of 16 GB and cut client DRAM demand.

title: Fiber delay-line carousel circulates weights past pipelined accelerators
idea: Combine 1950s delay-line memory with WDM optics: model weights circulate continuously in a 10-20 km amplified fiber loop at ~25 Tb/s aggregate, and each pipeline-stage accelerator taps the wavelengths carrying its layer exactly when they pass, so weights are stored in flight instead of in DRAM.
why: Holds ~150-300 MB per loop with zero lithography; fits strictly sequential weight streaming, though the ~50-100 us lap latency rules out random access.

title: Minify scientific arrays with in-line error-bounded lossy compression
idea: Minify smooth numeric data (simulation grids, time series, climate fields) using an SZ/ZFP-class error-bounded predictive compressor in the memory controller. Users set an absolute error bound per allocation.
why: 10-50x for scientific and HPC arrays at guaranteed error, so the same nodes run 10x larger problems.

title: Stranded-memory exchange: hourly auction of idle DRAM across tenants
idea: Po: your memory belongs to your neighbor. Cloud hosts expose DRAM left stranded when cores sell out first (typically 25-50%) into a CXL pool, and an exchange auctions it hourly to tenants' elastic caches under preemption contracts with posted prices.
why: Turns stranded capacity into supply; recovering half the stranded share raises usable fleet memory ~15-25% with zero new wafers.

title: Mole lives underground: vector search fully inside SSD controllers
idea: A mole never needs the surface. Billion-scale vector indexes (a graph ANN plus PQ codes, normally hundreds of GB of DRAM) live entirely on SSDs whose controllers walk the graph and compute PQ distances internally. The host keeps only a tiny entry-point table and receives top-k IDs.
why: This removes 90%+ of the DRAM in RAG and vector-database servers, where DRAM now costs ~20-40x flash per byte, at retrieval-acceptable millisecond latency.

title: Turn off memory mirroring and rank sparing; checkpoint in software
idea: Box: remove redundancy × BIOS RAS settings × channel/rank × fleet policy × application checkpoint and replication. Servers configured for mirroring (50% of capacity lost) or rank sparing (12–25%) are switched to full capacity, with reliability provided by software checkpoints and service-level replication.
why: Reclaims stranded capacity on installed hardware immediately; configuration only, no fluorinated inputs.

title: Epigenetic masks: tenant model variants as methylation over shared base
idea: Like methylation silencing genes without changing DNA, each customer fine-tune is stored as a sparse binary mask plus per-row scales over one shared base model, applied on the fly inside the matmul kernel instead of keeping a full copy.
why: Serving 1,000 variants needs one base plus ~1/16-size masks each instead of 1,000 copies; order-of-magnitude weight-memory savings in multi-tenant serving.

title: Developmental biologist: thousands of fine-tunes as epigenetic bit-masks
idea: Every cell shares one genome and differs only in which genes are switched on. Thousands of fine-tuned variants are served from one base copy in HBM. Each variant is stored as a run-length-coded sparse sign-flip/zero mask of about 0.1 bit per parameter or less, applied on the fly inside the matmul kernel.
why: This replaces per-tenant full copies or large adapters. 1,000 variants of a 70B model fit in roughly the memory of 1.1 copies, a 100x+ saving for multi-tenant serving.

title: HICAMP, fixed: content-addressed dedup hidden inside a CXL memory device
idea: Stanford's HICAMP stored memory as deduplicated immutable 64 B lines linked in DAGs but died because it needed a new CPU and programming model. Implement it inside a CXL expander that presents a flat address space: writes hash each line, a line-ID table maps addresses to unique content, and reference counts free lines, so VM images, checkpoints and string-heavy heaps dedup with zero software change.
why: Dedup ratios of 1.5-4x on VM/container fleets and multi-model serving cut physical DRAM per workload with no ISA change.

title: Gang-swapped tenants: time-share whole memory images like CPU cores
idea: Po: only one program exists at a time. Low-duty-cycle VMs, notebooks and agents are gang-scheduled: each entire memory image is snapshotted to CXL-flash and restored in tens of milliseconds at 50+ GB/s when its slot comes, so host DRAM is sized for the active set, not all tenants.
why: Dev boxes, notebooks and agents idle >90% of the time; time-multiplexing their DRAM cuts provisioned memory 3-5x for those fleets.

title: Mythic analog flash CIM, fixed: only cold MoE experts
idea: Mythic's analog flash compute-in-memory went bankrupt in 2022 on ADC overhead, drift and dense models outgrowing the chip. Narrow it to rarely-activated MoE experts: they live as conductances in NOR flash arrays and compute in place, while hot experts and attention stay digital, and the low duty cycle leaves time for drift recalibration.
why: Cold expert weights (often 80%+ of an MoE's bytes) never occupy DRAM/HBM.

title: Swap DRAM-blind procurement for mandatory memory-per-workload efficiency labels
idea: Substitute 'buy more RAM' with buyer pressure on software. Government and large-enterprise procurement require a measured GB-per-active-user or GB-per-transaction label under a standard benchmark (an Energy Star equivalent), give preference points to the top quartile, and require shared runtimes instead of a bundled browser engine per app.
why: Software bloat drives DRAM demand. Pressure on a few large vendors could cut client and server footprints 10-30% within one refresh cycle, with zero hardware change.

title: Via-programmed mask ROM stores frozen foundation-model weights
idea: Combine core-rope / mask-ROM hard-wiring with LLM deployment: a frozen base model's quantized weights are encoded in one via layer of a 40-65 nm DUV logic process (one transistor or less per bit, multi-level via codes) next to the compute array, while only LoRA adapters and KV use writable DRAM.
why: Removes weights from DRAM entirely for stable models using only mature DUV processes; only the via mask changes per model, so NRE stays low.

title: Miura-fold addressing: store mirrored structures once, unfold in hardware
idea: Origami packs a large sheet into a small footprint using a fold map. An address-fold unit in the memory controller recognizes registered fold regions (symmetric, Toeplitz, circulant, block-repeated, palindromic) and maps each virtual access through a fold function, for example (i,j)->(min,max) for symmetric or (i-j) for Toeplitz. Only the fundamental domain is stored physically, and writes stay consistent automatically.
why: Saves 2x on symmetric matrices (covariance, Hessians, undirected graphs, distance matrices) and N-fold on Toeplitz and relative-position-bias tables, with no change to software that indexes the full array.

title: Resistor weights from Minnesota: ReRAM compute tiles on SkyWater 130
idea: Po: the resistor is the weight. ReRAM integrated into SkyWater's Bloomington (MN) 130 nm flow stores edge and agent-model weights as multi-level conductances in crossbars that do matrix-vector products in place with on-chip ADCs, so weights never touch DRAM.
why: A DUV-only, trusted U.S. fab with no EUV runs small models DRAM-free, removing weight-fetch energy and DRAM footprint for edge fleets.

title: Sundial: leaky back-end TFT capacitors timestamp page age
idea: A sundial tells time without gears: give each 2 MB region a back-end IGZO TFT 'age capacitor' recharged on access that leaks predictably; the controller reads its voltage to rank regions for compression or demotion, getting LRU age from physics with zero DRAM bits or counter traffic.
why: Cheap, good-enough aging lets compression/tiering pick victims well, raising off-DRAM footprint by 10-20 points; back-end only.

title: Printed OECT ionic film stores on-device learned personalization
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): printed organic electrochemical transistors (PEDOT:PSS channels) store adapter weights as ionic doping levels that gated training pulses adjust, so a wearable or phone keeps and updates its personal adapter in a laminated film rather than in DRAM or in per-user memory on a server.
why: Per-user adapters and state at scale occupy device and server DRAM; ionic printed storage moves them into film costing cents per device.

title: Eliminate new DRAM purchases: CXL boards that re-home retired DDR4
idea: A small hardware team designs a CXL Type-3 card around an off-the-shelf CXL memory controller with 8 DDR4 slots and builds a test-and-bin line, turning DIMMs from decommissioned servers into a far-memory tier.
why: Avoids buying new DDR5 at 4x prices for cold tiers and gives ~5-year-old DRAM another 5 years of use, with no fab involved.

title: Scrap-metal dealer: memory-recovery contractor paid in reclaimed gigabytes
idea: Scrap dealers profit from what others throw away. A 6-person firm audits client fleets (heap dumps, page census, configs), applies the fixes, and keeps 30% of the first year's avoided DRAM purchases, verified by telemetry. The $1M covers runway until the first two contracts pay.
why: Most enterprises have 20-40% reclaimable memory but no team to get it. At 4x prices, gain-sharing makes adoption risk-free and unlocks supply without fabs.

title: NOR flash analog arrays compute FFN layers in place
idea: Combine 40 nm embedded NOR flash cells with analog matrix-vector multiplication: transformer feed-forward weights (~2/3 of parameters) are programmed as cell conductances and compute in place, while attention and KV stay digital in a small DRAM.
why: FFN weights never occupy DRAM; 40-55 nm NOR is DUV-only and domestically fabbable, though accuracy is limited by analog noise and drift.

title: Eliminate DRAM from inference: model pipelined across FPGA SRAM boards
idea: A small team builds a chassis of off-the-shelf FPGAs linked by serial transceivers; each FPGA holds a slice of a quantized model entirely in its on-chip URAM/BRAM, and tokens stream through the pipeline with no external DRAM.
why: No DRAM or HBM in the bill of materials for small and mid models; all data movement is on-chip at about 0.1 pJ/bit instead of 3-20 pJ/bit.

title: PCI-class hardware RAM Doubler card for cold pages
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out: take compression out of the latency path entirely; a 180 nm bus-master card (PCI-X/PCIe gen1 class, ~1 GB/s) compresses only pages idle >1 s with an LZ-class engine and packs them into a compressed DRAM pool, which the OS uses like zswap with hardware offload, echoing 1996's RAM Doubler.
why: Cold-page churn is ~10-100 MB/s per server, well within 1990s bandwidth; 20-40% more effective DRAM with no CPU cycles spent.

title: Garbage collector compresses cold object subgraphs behind forwarding stubs
idea: Box: compression × managed-runtime GC × object subgraph × untouched for N cycles × read-barrier inflate. During marking the runtime serializes cold subgraphs into compressed blobs and installs stubs; a read barrier inflates them on first touch.
why: Managed heaps run 2–5× larger than live data and much of it is cold; cold-object compression cuts heap 30–50%.

title: Mycologist's spores: hibernate idle AI agents as compressed snapshots
idea: Fungi survive lean times as tiny spores. Agent sessions spend most of their wall-clock time waiting on users or tools. After ~2 s idle, the session's KV cache, runtime heap and sandbox are snapshotted into a compressed, deduplicated spore on NVMe and rehydrated in tens of ms by lazily paging in only the pages touched first.
why: Agent fleets keep thousands of mostly idle sessions resident. Spores cut resident DRAM/HBM per concurrent agent 10-20x.

title: Thousand-tab browser freezing: pixels now, DOM later
idea: From the power user with 1,000 open tabs: background tabs and apps are frozen into a compressed render snapshot plus serialized semantic state (scroll, form fields, JS heap roots); DOM, layout trees and JIT heaps are freed and rebuilt lazily only when the user returns, while the snapshot displays instantly.
why: Browsers and Electron apps dominate client DRAM; freezing idle tabs removes 60-90% of their footprint, so an 8 GB laptop behaves like a 32 GB one.

title: Ebbinghaus forgetting curve: KV cache that evicts by natural decay
idea: Borrowed from human memory, where recall strengthens traces and neglect lets them fade: KV entries live in refresh-free DRAM where every attention read restores the row's charge, so attended tokens persist and ignored tokens decay; a per-row parity bit flags decayed entries, which attention masks out as forgotten.
why: Both the eviction policy and refresh disappear: zero refresh power, and the KV footprint self-limits to the actively attended set (often 10-30% of tokens).

title: Fractional-reserve memory: oversell DRAM with a lender of last resort
idea: Po: memory banks lend memory like money. Hypervisors sell 1.5x physical DRAM based on a model of peak co-occurrence across VMs, backed by a compressed-memory plus CXL-flash central-bank tier that absorbs runs, with priced insurance for tenants wanting guaranteed residency.
why: VM memory is reserved at peak but used at average (often 40-60%); controlled overcommit yields ~30-50% more sellable memory per DIMM.

title: Embargoed Soviet tinkerer: CXL tier built from scrapped DDR4 DIMMs
idea: With no new chips available, the tinkerer reuses old ones. Off-the-shelf FPGA CXL boards (~$5-10k each) each host 8-16 decommissioned DDR4 RDIMMs, burned in and binned by error rate, and expose them as a CXL Type-3 warm tier; firmware adds patrol scrubbing and thermal throttling. Budget: ~$400k for boards and lab, ~$600k for two FPGA/firmware engineers over 24 months.
why: Hyperscalers retire millions of DDR4 DIMMs. Reclaimed bits cost ~5-10% of new DDR5 at shortage prices and add 1.5-2x capacity per server for warm data.

title: Minify exact state to sketches: sketch-first analytics engine
idea: Minify exact hash aggregations, distinct counts, quantiles and join estimates to HyperLogLog, Count-Min and KLL sketches carrying explicit error bars. Exact recomputation from flash happens only when the query demands it.
why: Those operators need 100-1000x less memory, and analytics clusters shrink >=10x in DRAM.

title: JIT profiler narrows object fields with deoptimizing guards
idea: Combine JIT profiling with value-range compression: the runtime observes that fields only hold small ranges (counters under 65k, few enum values, pointers within one region) and rewrites class layouts to 16-, 8- or 2-bit fields, falling back to wide layouts when a guard catches an overflow.
why: Object-heavy services could shrink heaps 30-50% with no source changes.

title: Roll-to-roll web: stream tiles depth-first through every layer
idea: Activations are treated like the web in a roll-to-roll line. Each input tile runs through all layers (or a deep stage) before the next tile enters, and the overlap 'splice' halos at tile edges are recomputed. Full feature maps are never written to DRAM; only a moving web of tiles stays in on-chip SRAM. The compiler picks tile size the way a line picks web width, trading halo recompute against buffer size.
why: Activation memory for vision, diffusion and video models falls 10-50x, and DRAM traffic for intermediate tensors (fact 5) mostly disappears, at a cost of about 5-15% extra compute.

title: Threads migrate to data so each cluster byte exists once
idea: Reverse data-to-compute: for read-mostly shared sets (embedding tables, graphs) each node holds a disjoint shard, and lightweight threads or continuations hop to the node that owns the next address (Emu-style migration) instead of every node caching replicas.
why: Removes N-fold replicas in clusters: 2-8x less total DRAM for recommendation and graph workloads.

title: Codec-native memory keeps media as compressed bitstreams
idea: Worsen: decode video, images and textures to raw pixels in DRAM. Flip: keep media as AV1/HEVC tile bitstreams in memory and decode tiles on demand in a controller-side codec block, so only the touched macroblocks are ever expanded.
why: Cost: 50-200x effective capacity for media pipelines, vision training and rendering; trades decode latency and lossy fidelity.

title: Toyota kanban: WIP tokens keep fused-operator intermediates on-chip
idea: Borrowed from kanban cards that cap work-in-progress between stations: a dataflow accelerator passes hardware kanban tokens between fused operator stages, and a producer may emit a tile only when its consumer returns a token, bounding every intermediate tensor to a fixed SRAM budget so activations never touch DRAM.
why: Intermediates (often 30-60% of inference/training DRAM capacity and traffic) stay in SRAM with zero refresh; DRAM need shrinks to weights and checkpoints.

title: Whole-block dataflow fusion keeps intermediates only in SRAM
idea: Inverts 'every operator writes its output to memory': a compiler fuses an entire transformer block (norm, QKV, attention, MLP) into one persistent streaming kernel that passes tiles core-to-core through on-chip SRAM, so intermediate activations never touch DRAM/HBM during inference.
why: Removes activation buffers and workspace (often 10-30% of inference memory) and the traffic they generate.

title: Neon closed shells: zero and constant lines never touch DRAM
idea: Neon's full electron shell makes it inert; the controller keeps a 2-bit tag per 64 B line (zero, repeated byte, repeated word, real) in a 0.4%-overhead table cached in controller SRAM, so writes of trivial lines only update the tag, reads are synthesized on chip, and the unused backing lines join a free pool.
why: ReLU/sparse activations, fresh allocations and padded tensors are 30-80% trivial lines; those accesses cost ~0.05 pJ/bit of SRAM tag lookup instead of 10-20 pJ/bit, averaging >=10x lower energy per access on sparse workloads and freeing the same share of capacity (energy, density).

title: Coat check ticket: park idle chat KV with recompute receipts
idea: Hand over the coat, keep a ticket: when a chat session idles >30 s its KV is cut to 2-bit and moved to flash, keeping only a ticket (token IDs plus which layers need exact recompute); on resume the engine recomputes the quality-critical layers and dequantizes the rest. Ships as serving firmware with no fabrication step.
why: Most sessions sit idle most of the time; KV DRAM held per user drops 10-30x.

title: Retired DDR4 reborn in CXL expanders as compressed far tier
idea: IFR: memory already mined is used forever. Constraint: no new extraction of W, Hf or Ta, so harvest DDR4 DIMMs from decommissioned servers, test and bin them, and mount them in CXL type-3 expanders behind an inline compressor as a far tier for cold pages.
why: Turns a waste stream into usable capacity, offsetting 20-30% of new DDR5 purchases in a refresh cycle with zero new scarce elements.

title: Procedural memory lines that store a generator, not data
idea: Worsen: store huge regular arrays (index ranges, constant fills, strided tables, LFSR masks) byte by byte. Flip: a line tag marks a line as procedural, holding a 16-byte micro-program (base, stride, affine coefficients or LFSR seed) that a tiny ALU in the controller expands on read; writes that break the pattern fall back to a normal line.
why: Capacity: 10-100x for pattern-heavy data such as position tables, masks, and initialization buffers; small gains overall but zero-cost when unused.

title: Grocery spoil-and-restock: refresh-free DRAM as clean-only cache
idea: Borrowed from produce departments that discard spoiled stock and restock from the warehouse: DRAM runs with refresh off and holds only clean copies whose master lives in CXL or flash; each row has weak 'canary' cells plus a CRC, a read that finds a tripped canary simply re-fetches, and dirty data stays in a small SRAM write buffer that writes through.
why: Zero refresh energy and 10-20% bandwidth back; the DRAM tier shrinks to a pure cache, and cells no longer need to meet the 64 ms tail spec, improving yield and cost.

title: Via-programmed mask ROM freezes model weights into old-node silicon
idea: TRIZ #36 Phase transition: freeze 'liquid' read-only weights into 'solid' via-programmed NOR/NAND mask ROM on 180 nm lines, where only one via mask changes per model, so frozen weights and vocabulary tables leave DRAM for cheap, refresh-free, one-transistor-per-bit storage.
why: Removes read-only data from DRAM for edge and embedded inference with zero refresh and cheap masks (~$20-50k); density of ~0.1-0.2 GB/cm2 limits it to small models.

title: Global Memory Service, fixed: a spot market for idle fleet DRAM
idea: UW's 1990s Global Memory Service paged to idle workstations' RAM but died on 10 Mb/s networks and owners' lack of incentive. With 400G RDMA, run an internal spot market where hosts post unused DRAM at a price, borrowers bid for 1 GB revocable leases, and the scheduler packs elastic jobs onto borrowed memory.
why: Clouds strand 25-50% of provisioned DRAM; pricing it unlocks that supply without buying new chips.

title: Bit-plane weight layout: one stored copy serves every precision tier
idea: Box: progressive precision × memory layout × bit-plane × per-request policy × MSB-first planes. Weights are stored as bit-planes so a request tier or insensitive layer fetches only the top k planes, replacing separate 8-, 4- and 3-bit copies of the same model.
why: Serving fleets keep 2–4 quantized copies per model; one progressive copy saves ~2–3× across a model zoo and cuts bytes read for low tiers.

title: Silver-ion drift integrators remember page heat across reboots
idea: Every 64 KB region gets a nanoscale Ag/electrolyte integrator. Each access pulse drifts a few silver ions, so conductance becomes a nonvolatile, slowly relaxing log of cumulative accesses. On boot or VM migration, the placement engine reads the map and pre-places hot data in DRAM and cold data in CXL/flash right away, instead of relearning for minutes.
why: Tiering is accurate from second zero, so providers can provision 20-30% less DRAM without cold-start penalties.

title: Sleep consolidation: agents distill yesterday's context into small adapters
idea: Po: yesterday's conversation becomes today's neurons. Long-lived agents compress their accumulated context nightly into a low-rank adapter (tens of MB) by self-distillation on U.S.-fabbed accelerators, discarding the GB-scale KV cache and keeping only a short summary window.
why: Persistent agent memory moves from O(context) KV (GBs) to O(1) adapters (MBs): 50-100x less memory for long-running agents.

title: Optical-multicast KV prefix CDN inside the rack
idea: Worsen: let every GPU hold its own KV copy of the same system prompt and RAG documents. Flip: a rack memory node stores each shared prefix's KV once and streams it to subscribing GPUs over an optical broadcast star, so GPUs keep only per-request suffix KV.
why: Capacity: 3-10x less HBM spent on duplicated prefix KV in agent and chat fleets with common prompts.

title: Swap full fine-tuned model copies for 1-bit deltas over one base
idea: Substitute per-customer full checkpoints with sign-bit delta matrices plus one scale per row, applied by a fused GEMM kernel over a single resident base model. Full-rank fine-tunes are covered, not just LoRAs, on existing GPUs.
why: Each 70B variant drops from ~140 GB to ~9 GB, a ~15x memory cut for multi-tenant model hosting.

title: Eliminate per-worker model copies via shared read-only weight mappings
idea: A serving framework loads weights once as a read-only mmap of safetensors files shared by all CPU workers, and shares a single GPU copy across worker processes using CUDA IPC handles, instead of each worker loading its own.
why: Multi-worker CPU and GPU serving often duplicates weights 4-16x per node; collapsing them to one copy saves most of that.

title: Glass-panel interposer lets accelerators share one memory set
idea: Weights are replicated per GPU only because off-package bandwidth is too poor to share them. A 510x515 mm glass-core panel interposer with 2 um RDL and through-glass vias places 8 accelerators around one common ring of memory stacks at near-local bandwidth, so tensor- and data-parallel groups read a single physical copy of the weights.
why: Weight replicas per 8-GPU group drop from 8 to 1-2, cutting HBM bits per deployment 30-60%; glass is low-loss and uses no silicon interposer wafers.

title: One-brain package: CPU and accelerator share memory, no staging copies
idea: Po: the CPU and the accelerator are the same animal. CPU and accelerator dies co-packaged with Foveros in New Mexico share one coherent pool of U.S.-made DRAM, eliminating duplicate pinned host buffers, dataloader staging copies and host-side mirrors of device tensors.
why: Discrete-accelerator hosts often carry 1-2x accelerator memory in host DRAM for staging; unification cuts host DRAM 30-50%.

title: Price LLM APIs per KV-gigabyte-second to shape context demand
idea: Box: demand shaping × API pricing × request × billing × KV-GB-second meter with shared-prefix discounts. Customers pay for the memory-time their context occupies, with discounts for shared prefixes and short sessions, nudging agents to summarize and reuse.
why: Makes the scarce resource visible to buyers; a 20–30% drop in average resident context is plausible using only billing logic, no fluorinated chemistry.

title: Swap fixed DIMM ownership for optically re-patched memory blades
idea: Substitute static wiring with a reconfigurable optical patch panel. Memory blades connect to servers through optical circuit switches, which reassign blades to servers every few minutes or hours following scheduler forecasts, so capacity physically follows demand.
why: Clouds strand ~25-35% of DRAM because each server is sized for its own peak. Moving capacity between servers cuts installed DRAM ~20% at equal service.

title: DRAM and NAND dies in one stack with self-tiering base die
idea: Combine a few older-node DRAM dies and several NAND dies in one bonded/TSV stack over a 28 nm logic base die that tracks page heat and migrates 4 KB pages between DRAM and NAND internally at TSV bandwidth, presenting one flat byte-addressable space.
why: Gives ~4-8x capacity per package from mostly DUV NAND bits; in-package migration avoids host-side tiering overhead and channel traffic.

title: Embargoed Soviet engineer: 32-bit compressed pointers everywhere via cage allocator
idea: Under embargo you rewrite the software to fit the machine you have. Compilers and allocators place each heap in a 4-32 GB 'cage' and store all heap pointers as shifted 32-bit offsets. The JVM and V8 already do this; a compiler flag plus ABI shim extends it to C++, Rust and Go.
why: Pointers are 20-40% of the heap in pointer-heavy services (graphs, trees, ORMs). Halving them cuts DRAM 10-25% fleet-wide with no new hardware.

title: Roll-to-roll printed ferroelectric polymer read-mostly memory tier
idea: Read-mostly data (embedding tables, checkpoints, search indexes) needs few writes, so 1e7-1e8 cycles of endurance is enough. Gravure-print ferroelectric-diode crossbars from a P(VDF-TrFE):semiconductor blend, which gives a non-destructive resistive read, onto PET film at roll-to-roll speed, and laminate many films into a stack.
why: R2R printing costs ~10,000x less per area than silicon, so even at microsecond access, offloading read-mostly bytes trims DRAM 20-40% in recommender and search fleets.

title: Boron icosahedra: succinct indexes with near-memory rank/select fit in SRAM
idea: Boron packs into compact 12-atom icosahedra; database and search indexes are rebuilt as succinct structures (Elias-Fano lists, wavelet trees, rank/select bitvectors) at 1-2 bits per element above entropy, and a near-memory unit adds single-cycle popcount-based rank/select so lookups stay fast.
why: Indexes shrink 5-20x so most fit in on-die SRAM or LLC, cutting energy per lookup >10x versus DRAM and freeing the DRAM they occupied (energy, density).

title: Precision-transcoding DIMM buffer for tagged ML address ranges
idea: TRIZ #3 Local quality: a 180 nm buffer chip on the module holds a small range table; writes to tagged ranges are converted FP32 to BF16 or FP16 to FP8 with stochastic rounding and stored packed into a half- or quarter-size physical region, and reads are expanded back, so precision varies by region with no software changes.
why: CPU-side ML data (embeddings, optimizer state, feature stores) is often FP32; 2-4x capacity on those ranges using simple 180 nm arithmetic.

title: Eliminate 3x replication in memory caches using erasure coding
idea: A drop-in memcached/Redis cluster proxy stripes values with Reed-Solomon RS(10,4) across nodes and decodes on the client, replacing triple replication for durable caches.
why: Memory overhead for fault tolerance falls from 3x to 1.4x, a 53% DRAM saving.

title: Holography: superpose thousands of associations in one SRAM hypervector
idea: Borrowed from holograms, where many images share one plate: older KV pairs are bound (permute-multiply or circular convolution) and summed into a fixed set of high-dimensional superposition vectors in SRAM, and attention queries unbind from them, with a small cleanup memory for exact recall of key items.
why: Bounded memory for unbounded context: a growing DRAM KV becomes fixed SRAM with zero refresh; the capacity-versus-noise trade-off is the risk.

title: Sparse 1-bit activation memory for inference
idea: Worsen: store activations as dense fp16. Flip: train networks whose stored activations are binary and 90% sparse, keeping them as run-length-coded bitmaps, so activation buffers shrink by 16x times 10x.
why: Cost: about 160x less activation memory; trades retraining and accuracy on hard tasks.

title: RDL side-port lets HBM time-slice between tenants in milliseconds
idea: One added redistribution-layer mask on the interposer routes a wide side-port from each HBM base die to a co-packaged flash/LPDDR tier. A tenant's entire 24 GB HBM context then swaps in about 5 ms without crossing the GPU, so HBM is time-shared among 3-4 low-duty inference tenants like CPU time slices.
why: HBM is allocated in time instead of space, so bursty low-duty serving needs 2-3x less HBM.

title: Swap live background-tab heaps for pixel-and-state snapshots
idea: Substitute a background tab's DOM and JS heap (often 100-500 MB) with a compressed screenshot plus URL, scroll position and form state. The browser rehydrates the tab by reload and state replay on focus, and service-worker caches make the reload fast. No hardware change.
why: Background tabs dominate client memory, so PCs could ship 8 GB instead of 16 GB for typical users, cutting client DRAM demand.

title: Near-memory collectives eliminate per-GPU staging buffers
idea: Worsen: allocate large send/receive staging buffers in every GPU for all-reduce and all-gather. Flip: execute reductions inside the CXL or NVLink-attached memory pool, so each GPU writes once into the pool and reads the reduced result back, with no per-GPU staging copies.
why: Capacity: frees 5-15% of HBM per accelerator used today for communication buffers, and cuts redundant traffic.

title: Laser-written diffractive glass embodies frozen network layers
idea: A fixed linear transform needs no stored bits if it is built into geometry. Write the frozen embedding projection or the early layers of vision and speech models as stacked phase plates in fused silica (femtosecond direct write); a microLED array encodes the inputs and photodiodes read the outputs, so those weights occupy no DRAM and need no refresh.
why: Weights and activations of frozen front-end layers leave DRAM in edge devices and high-volume serving, and energy per MAC is near zero because propagating light does the work.

title: Clonal-selection antibody codebook compresses frequent cache-line patterns
idea: The memory controller keeps a 4K-entry 'antibody repertoire' of 64-byte line patterns; a line matching an antibody within a few bit flips is stored as a 12-bit pointer plus a sparse mutation mask. Antibodies that match often are cloned and hypermutated into variants and unused ones die, so the codebook evolves per workload like adaptive immunity.
why: Effective capacity: adaptive line-level compression, 1.5-3x on weights, page tables and zero-heavy activations, no software changes.

title: Time-multiplex accelerator HBM between inference peaks and training troughs
idea: TRIZ #20 Continuity of useful action: the same HBM pool hosts serving KV caches at diurnal peaks and fine-tuning/eval activations at night, with sub-minute handoff via sharded checkpoints to CXL/flash, so no byte sits idle 12 hours a day.
why: Inference fleets average ~30-50% memory use; shrinks the separate training-memory fleet by 20-40%.

title: Interchangeable parts: snap near-duplicate float lines to standard gauges
idea: Interchangeable parts came from making every part to a gauge tolerance. A line-level 'gauge dedup' engine hashes float lines after rounding to a per-region tolerance, using a locality-sensitive hash on the top mantissa bits. Lines within tolerance map to one canonical stored line, while regions flagged as precise get exact dedup only.
why: Model checkpoints, ensembles, fine-tune variants, simulation snapshots and gradient histories hold many near-identical lines that exact dedup misses, so tiers holding them gain 1.5-4x capacity.
